templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
Items in a series (commas; semicolons when items contain commas)
No punctuation inside a compound joined by and
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element
No punctuation between subject and verb
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a prepositional opener
items.passage: During World War II, British inventor Geoffrey Pyke proposed building enormous aircraft carriers from a frozen mixture of water and wood ______ ordinary ice, which shatters easily under impact, the composite material, later named pykrete, proved highly resistant to gunfire in tests and melted considerably more slowly.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “a frozen mixture of water and wood pulp.” The second sentence opens with the phrase “Unlike ordinary ice, which shatters easily under impact,” which compares ice with the sentence’s subject, “the composite material,” whose verbs are “proved” and “melted.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma attaches “unlike ordinary ice ...” to the first sentence, so the main clause “the composite material ... proved highly resistant” is joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: “That” begins a clause describing the pulp, but the words that follow already have their own subject, “the composite material,” and verb, so the sentence becomes ungrammatical.

D.why_wrong: With no mark, “unlike ordinary ice” attaches to “wood pulp” in the first clause, and the main clause “the composite material ... proved highly resistant” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: science and technology (materials, World War II engineering). Band-6 shape (3.4, 886dc9f9): clause 2 opens with an 8-word prepositional phrase that a comma or no mark glues onto clause 1’s last noun; the subject of clause 2 arrives 9 words after the blank and its verb, “proved,” 15 words after it. One-sentence run. Real subject known well (Pyke’s 1942 proposal, Project Habakkuk); no other names.

band7.why: 8-word prepositional opener (“Unlike ordinary ice, which shatters ...”) that can trail clause 1; the subject comes 9 words past the blank; a prepositional opener is the band-6 type (aab74a3b, 886dc9f9); wrong options all fail on rule, as targeted.

review.note: Writer flagged topic fame (pykrete); knowing it does not help with the boundary, so kept. Pyke’s proposal and the test results are the standard record.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a past-participle opener
items.passage: In 1851, the ruler of Khiva, in present-day Uzbekistan, commissioned what was intended to become the tallest minaret in the Islamic world, but construction ceased abruptly in 1855, when he was killed in ______ incomplete at about 29 meters, the tower, now called Kalta Minor, is decorated with bands of glazed tilework.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “when he was killed in battle.” The second sentence opens with the participial phrase “Left incomplete at about 29 meters,” which describes its subject, “the tower,” and then gives the main verb “is decorated.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: The comma attaches “left incomplete at about 29 meters” to the first sentence, so the main clause “the tower ... is decorated with bands of glazed tilework” is joined to it with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “And left” makes the phrase a second action of the ruler (“was killed in battle and left ...”), so the main clause “the tower ... is decorated” is still joined to the first sentence with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no mark, “left incomplete ...” runs into the first sentence, and the main clause “the tower ... is decorated” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: history (Central Asian architecture). Band-6 shape (1b97cce9 menu: period, comma, and, none): a 5-word past-participle opener; the splice appears at “the tower ... is decorated,” 13 words after the blank, behind the appositive “now called Kalta Minor”; the run is one 52-word sentence.

fixes: register: “approximately 29 meters” to “about 29 meters” in passage, explanation and why_wrong B (hard tier ran 5.34 chars/word, CB 5.17)

band7.why: 5-word past-participle opener, subject “the tower” 7 words past the blank; 1b97cce9 menu (comma, and, none); opener under the band-7 floor of 8 words, as targeted.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long noun-phrase opener
items.passage: In 1938, workers digging the foundation of a house in Ile-Ife, Nigeria, unearthed more than a dozen copper-alloy ______ of such naturalistic detail that some European scholars questioned their African origin, the sculptures had been cast by Yoruba artists roughly six centuries earlier.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “unearthed more than a dozen copper-alloy heads.” The second sentence opens with the noun phrase “Works of such naturalistic detail that some European scholars questioned their African origin,” which describes its subject, “the sculptures,” and then gives the main verb “had been cast.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma makes “works of such naturalistic detail ...” an appositive describing the heads, so the main clause “the sculptures had been cast ...” is joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “heads works of such naturalistic detail” runs two noun phrases together, and the main clause “the sculptures had been cast ...” still follows the first main clause with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: “Which were works” turns the phrase into a description of the heads inside the first sentence, so the main clause “the sculptures had been cast ...” is still joined to it with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: arts (West African sculpture). Band-7 checks (band7/boundaries.md section 6): opener of 13 words, a noun-phrase appositive whose that-clause has its own finite verb (“questioned”), so it reads naturally on clause 1’s last noun in A, B and C; the splice shows only at “the sculptures had been cast,” 15 words after the blank; one-sentence run of 43 words; reasoning steps 3. Real subject known well (Wunmonije compound finds, 1938).
band7_moves: opener of 13 words, a noun-phrase appositive (940ff6f7, 3.8) that could describe clause 1’s last noun
the opener’s that-clause has a finite verb, so it looks like a clause
comma, glued and which-were options hold until the splice 15 words after the blank

band7.why: 13-word noun-phrase appositive opener with its own that-clause that reads naturally on “heads” in A, B and C; the splice shows only at “the sculptures had been cast,” 15 words past the blank; 940ff6f7 / 4b424102 menu (comma, glued, which-were).

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing the first clause, contrast with the previous sentence
items.passage: When astronomers analyze the light of a star, they typically detect plenty of iron, one of the most common heavy elements in stars. The spectrum of Przybylski’s star, first examined in 1961, tells a different ______ it contains remarkably little iron but unexpectedly strong signatures of rare elements such as holmium.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “However” contrasts Przybylski’s star with the stars described in the first sentence, so it belongs with the first clause: “The spectrum of Przybylski’s star ... tells a different story, however.” The semicolon after “however” then joins this main clause to the second one, “it contains remarkably little iron ...,” which explains what the different story is.

A.why_wrong: The commas set off “however” but leave the two main clauses (“The spectrum ... tells a different story” and “it contains remarkably little iron ...”) joined with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: Placing “however” after the semicolon makes it introduce the second clause, signaling a contrast between “tells a different story” and “it contains remarkably little iron ...”; but the second clause explains the different story rather than contrasting with it.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation before “however,” the two main clauses run together with no mark at their boundary.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (astronomy). Band-7 checks: adverb closes clause 1 and answers the previous sentence (b771d175, be37d4ae); the textbook “; however,” fails only on meaning, against a sentence that ends 12 words before the blank (logic-wrong distractor, cue outside a 6-word window); reasoning steps 4. Real subject known well.
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1 and contrasts with the previous sentence
logic-wrong distractor: the textbook “; however,” placement
the deciding contrast lies in the previous sentence, outside a 6-word window

band7.why: b771d175 / be37d4ae move and menu: “however” closes clause 1, which answers the previous sentence; the taught “; however,” (C) fails only on meaning, since clause 2 explains the different story; the cue sits in the previous sentence.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening the second clause (rather)
items.passage: Euclides da Cunha first traveled to Canudos, a settlement in the northeastern backlands of Brazil, as a correspondent covering a military campaign against its inhabitants. Os Sertões (1902), the book he subsequently wrote, is not simply a war ______ its opening sections examine the region’s geology, climate, and population, and the fighting appears only afterward.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Rather” signals that the second clause corrects the first: the book is not simply a war report; instead, its opening sections examine the region’s land and people. A semicolon joins the two main clauses (“Os Sertões ... is not simply a war report” and “its opening sections examine ...”), and the comma after “rather” sets the adverb off from the clause it introduces.

A.why_wrong: The commas around “rather” leave the two main clauses joined with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no mark before “rather,” the two main clauses run together without the punctuation needed between them.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two main clauses “Os Sertões ... is not simply a war report” and “its opening sections examine ....”

items.notes: Subject: literature (Brazilian nonfiction). Band-6 shape (3.5): “not simply X; rather, Y,” with the adverb opening clause 2; the option set adds a bare comma splice and a fused “rather” instead of a second semicolon placement. Real subject known well.

band7.why: “; rather,” opening clause 2 (3.5 / a9e5b788 shape); every wrong option fails on rule; band 7 never uses rather.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase with a relative clause
items.passage: In 1929, researchers at Istanbul’s Topkapı Palace discovered a fragment of a world map that the Ottoman admiral Piri Reis had compiled on gazelle-skin parchment in 1513. Notes written on the map identify one of its most unexpected ______ navigational chart that, according to the admiral, had been drawn by Christopher Columbus and has never been found.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Notes written on the map identify one of its most unexpected sources” is a complete main clause, and what follows, “a navigational chart that, according to the admiral, had been drawn by Christopher Columbus and has never been found,” is a noun phrase that specifies which source is meant. A colon correctly introduces this explanation.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “a navigational chart that ... has never been found” has no main verb of its own; “had been drawn” and “has never been found” belong to the “that” clause.

C.why_wrong: “It was a navigational chart ...” is a second main clause, and the comma alone can’t join it to the first main clause, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: The period leaves “A navigational chart that, according to the admiral, had been drawn by Christopher Columbus and has never been found.” as a fragment: its only finite verbs belong to the “that” clause.

items.notes: Subject: history (Ottoman cartography). Band-7 checks: clause ends in an announcing phrase (“one of its most unexpected sources”); the explanation is a noun phrase whose that-clause is interrupted by “according to the admiral” and then carries finite verbs (“had been drawn,” “has never been found”), so the period and semicolon versions look like full sentences (e9aee0d8 shape, “that, facilitating ..., helped”); comma + “it was” decoy as in e9aee0d8; no lone-dash option; run 30 words. Real subject known well.
band7_moves: noun phrase after the colon contains a relative clause with a finite verb, so the semicolon and period options look complete

fixes: hardened toward e9aee0d8: the noun phrase after the colon now carries a comma-set interrupter and two finite verbs (“that, according to the admiral, had been drawn by Christopher Columbus and has never been found”), run 24 to 30 words, so the period and semicolon versions read more like sentences; “researchers cataloging the library of” to “researchers at” to keep the passage at the models’ length (57 words); “Annotations in the map’s margins” to “Notes written on the map” (Piri Reis’s notes are spread over the map); explanation and why_wrong B and D updated

band7.why: After the fix, e9aee0d8 move and menu: announcing clause, colon, then a noun phrase whose that-clause is interrupted by “according to the admiral” and carries two finite verbs, so the period and semicolon versions look like sentences; 30-word run, shorter than the 40 to 55 of the S2_colon officials, so the verdict rests on the disguised-fragment distractors, the signal that matters for this template. Before the fix the short relative clause made both fragments plain (band 6).

review.note: Writer flagged topic fame (Piri Reis map); knowing the map does not help place the colon, so kept. Columbus chart among the sources is Piri Reis’s own note, read right from recall.

items.subtype: No punctuation around a restrictive non-person appositive in the subject
items.passage: Many planktonic animals are nearly transparent, which helps them hide from predators. Males of the ______ take a different approach: tiny crystals stacked inside their skin cells make their backs shimmer in brilliant blue, violet, or gold, though at certain angles the animals seem to disappear.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Sapphirina metallina” identifies which copepod the sentence is about; without it, “the copepod” could be any of thousands of species. Because the name is essential, no punctuation should set it off from “copepod,” and no punctuation belongs between the subject (“Males of the copepod Sapphirina metallina”) and its verb, “take.”

A.why_wrong: The comma separates the essential name from “copepod,” as if the name were extra information, although it is needed to identify the animal.

B.why_wrong: The comma separates the subject, “Males of the copepod Sapphirina metallina,” from its verb, “take.”

D.why_wrong: The pair of commas marks the name as nonessential, but the sentence needs it to say which copepod is meant.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (marine biology). Band-7 checks: non-person restrictive appositive after “the” + a category noun (59a246dc), here in the subject so a comma before the verb is also tempting; the comma pair looks polite; local rule (S4_restrictive is exempt from the window check). Real subject known well.
band7_moves: restrictive appositive that is not a person (the copepod X), after “the”
long subject before the verb so a comma after the name looks natural

band7.why: 59a246dc exactly: a non-person restrictive appositive after “the” plus a category noun, same four-option menu, here in the subject so the comma before the verb also tempts; local rule, exempt from the window check.

items.subtype: No punctuation with a restrictive that-clause in a long subject
items.passage: In a 2007 study, behavioral scientist Uri Simonsohn looked at how admissions readers at a selective university scored hundreds of applicants. The ______ placed more weight on academic achievements and less on outside activities, a pattern captured in the paper’s title, “Clouds Make Nerds Look Good.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: ratings that readers gave on cloudy days,
ratings that readers gave on cloudy days
ratings, that readers gave on cloudy days,
ratings, that readers gave on cloudy days
items.explanation: The clause “that readers gave on cloudy days” is essential: it tells which ratings placed more weight on academic achievements. A restrictive clause beginning with “that” takes no commas, and no comma belongs between the subject (“The ratings that readers gave on cloudy days”) and its verb, “placed.”

A.why_wrong: The comma separates the subject, “The ratings that readers gave on cloudy days,” from its verb, “placed.”

C.why_wrong: The commas treat “that readers gave on cloudy days” as extra information, but the clause is needed to identify which ratings are meant, and a “that” clause is never set off with commas.

D.why_wrong: The comma before “that” wrongly separates “ratings” from the restrictive clause that identifies them.

items.notes: Subject: social science (judgment and decision making). Band-6 shape (6181924a): the subject is a noun plus a restrictive that-clause, and the options vary commas at two slots. Real study known well (Simonsohn 2007, admissions ratings weighted academics more on cloudier days); the quoted words are the paper’s title.

band7.why: 6181924a shape: restrictive that-clause in a long subject, commas varied at two slots; no band-7 move, as targeted.

review.note: Real named researcher with his real finding and paper title (Simonsohn 2007, J. Behav. Decis. Making), read right from recall; nothing made up is attributed to him.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: comma plus but, second clause opening with a phrase
items.passage: Serpent Mound, an earthen snake effigy in Ohio, was traditionally attributed to the Adena culture and dated to around 300 BCE. Radiocarbon measurements from the 1990s pointed instead to the considerably later Fort Ancient ______ in 2014, a reanalysis of sediment reaffirmed the earlier date.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence joins two main clauses: “Radiocarbon measurements from the 1990s pointed instead to the considerably later Fort Ancient culture” and “in 2014, a reanalysis of sediment reaffirmed the earlier date.” A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them, and “but” fits the contrast between the two findings.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two main clauses; without a conjunction, the result is a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: When “but” joins two long main clauses such as these, a comma is needed before it.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together, and “in 2014” seems to belong to the first one.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (North America). Planned band_target 7, but S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items (band7/boundaries.md, assignment table), so written as a strong band 6 per WAVE.md: clause 2 opens with “in 2014,” which a fused or no-comma reading attaches to clause 1 (7ce4ee13). Real subject known well (Adena attribution, 1990s Fort Ancient dates, 2014 reanalysis).

band7.why: S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items, so a strong band 6 at most: “in 2014,” opens clause 2 and a fused or no-comma reading attaches it to clause 1 (7ce4ee13).

items.subtype: Semicolons between list items that contain commas
items.passage: Making a Tibetan thangka, a Buddhist painting on cloth, involves several careful stages: priming the cotton canvas with gesso and burnishing it with a smooth ______ pigments from minerals such as malachite, azurite, and cinnabar; and outlining deities on a geometric grid that fixes their proportions.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The colon introduces a list of three stages, and the second stage contains commas of its own (“malachite, azurite, and cinnabar”). Semicolons must therefore separate the items, as the semicolon after “cinnabar” shows. A semicolon after “stone” correctly separates the first stage from the second.

B.why_wrong: A comma here doesn’t match the semicolon that separates the second stage from the third; when list items contain commas, semicolons must separate all of the items.

C.why_wrong: A colon can’t separate two items in a list; the colon after “stages” has already introduced the list.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “stone grinding pigments” runs the first and second stages together.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Tibetan painting). Band-6 shape (c49e946e: items; managing): three gerund-phrase stages, blank after item 1, the revealing semicolon comes 10 words after the blank. Real subject known well.

band7.why: c49e946e shape: blank after item 1, revealing semicolon 10 words later; a single slot with no second rule inside the option, so band 6 as targeted.

items.subtype: No punctuation between two parts of a compound object joined by and
items.passage: Composed around the fourth century BCE, the Aṣṭādhyāyī of the Sanskrit grammarian Pāṇini codifies the language in nearly 4,000 concise rules. Linguists today still admire how systematically these rules specify the way words are assembled from smaller meaningful ______ and the way those words are combined into sentences.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank falls inside a compound object: the rules specify “the way words are assembled from smaller meaningful units” and “the way those words are combined into sentences.” Two elements joined by “and” in this way take no punctuation between them.

A.why_wrong: A comma before “and” wrongly separates the two parts of the compound object of “specify.”

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “and the way those words are combined into sentences” is not a main clause.

D.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete idea that it introduces; here it would interrupt the compound object of “specify.”

items.notes: Subject: language (Sanskrit grammar). Band-6 shape (3.3): the blank ends the first of two parallel noun phrases joined by “and,” after a long how-clause, so a comma feels natural. Real subject known well.

fixes: “Composed ..., the Sanskrit grammarian Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī codifies” to “Composed ..., the Aṣṭādhyāyī of the Sanskrit grammarian Pāṇini codifies” (the opener read as describing the grammarian)

band7.why: S4_compound has no band-7 official items; 3.3 shape, the comma tempts after a long how-clause; strong band 6.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: comma plus but
items.passage: Breaking a dress code is generally assumed to damage a person’s reputation. A 2014 study by business researchers found that such nonconformity can lead observers to judge a person as more competent and higher in ______ the effect appeared only when observers believed the person had broken the code on purpose.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence joins two main clauses: “A 2014 study ... found that such nonconformity can lead observers to judge a person as more competent and higher in status” and “the effect appeared only when observers believed ....” A comma followed by “but” correctly joins them, and “but” marks the limit placed on the finding.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two main clauses; without a conjunction, the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: When “but” joins two long main clauses such as these, a comma is needed before it.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together.

items.notes: Subject: social science (consumer psychology). Standard comma-conjunction menu (splice, fused, conjunction without comma). Real study described without names (Bellezza, Gino and Keinan 2014, the red sneakers effect, which depends on the nonconformity seeming deliberate).

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a short introductory phrase
items.passage: Around the second century CE, the Chola king Karikalan had a dam of unhewn boulders built across the Kaveri River to redirect its seasonal floodwaters toward agricultural land in southern ______ two thousand years later, the structure, known as the Kallanai, still channels water into a network of irrigation canals.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “toward agricultural land in southern India.” The second sentence opens with the phrase “Nearly two thousand years later,” followed by its subject, “the structure,” and its verb, “channels.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: The comma joins the main clause “the structure ... still channels water ...” to the first main clause without a conjunction, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no mark, “nearly two thousand years later” attaches to the first clause, and the main clause “the structure ... still channels water” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “And” joins the two main clauses without the comma that should come before it.

items.notes: Subject: history and technology (South Asian irrigation). Medium shape (2.27): a short time phrase opens clause 2, the subject arrives 5 words after the blank. Real subject known well.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: The jade vine, a climbing plant native to the rainforests of the Philippines, bears claw-shaped flowers of an extraordinary blue-green color. Its blossoms hang in clusters up to three meters long, dangling beneath the forest ______ them accessible to the nectar-feeding bats that pollinate the vine.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause “Its blossoms hang in clusters up to three meters long, dangling beneath the forest canopy” is followed by the participial phrase “making them accessible to the nectar-feeding bats that pollinate the vine,” which describes a result of the way the blossoms hang. A comma correctly separates the main clause from this trailing phrase.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “making them accessible to the nectar-feeding bats ...” is a phrase with no subject or main verb.

B.why_wrong: The period leaves “Making them accessible to the nectar-feeding bats that pollinate the vine.” as a fragment; its only finite verb, “pollinate,” belongs to the “that” clause.

C.why_wrong: Without a comma, “making them accessible ...” seems to describe the forest canopy rather than the hanging blossoms.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (botany, pollination). Medium shape (2.4, 2.26): main clause plus an -ing phrase that states a result, with the standard semicolon, period and missing-comma decoys. Real subject known well (Strongylodon macrobotrys, bat-pollinated).

items.subtype: Closing a comma pair around an appositive
items.passage: Persian miniature paintings often illustrate scenes from famous poems and histories. Kamoliddin Behzod, the leading painter at the court of Sultan Husayn Bayqara in ______ became renowned for filling such scenes with ordinary people who build, argue, and gesture in lifelike ways.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The appositive “the leading painter at the court of Sultan Husayn Bayqara in Herat” interrupts the main clause “Kamoliddin Behzod ... became renowned ....” It opens with a comma after “Behzod,” so it must close with a matching comma after “Herat.”

A.why_wrong: A semicolon can’t close the appositive; it would cut off the subject, “Kamoliddin Behzod,” from its verb, “became.”

B.why_wrong: The appositive opens with a comma, so it can’t be closed with a dash.

D.why_wrong: Without a closing comma, the appositive opened after “Behzod” is never closed.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Timurid painting). Medium shape (2.1): the partner comma sits 11 words before the blank, after the subject. Real subject known well.

items.subtype: Comma after a long introductory participial phrase
items.passage: Compiled in 712 CE by the scholar Ō no Yasumaro from myths, legends, and genealogies that a court attendant named Hieda no Are had memorized and ______ Kojiki is the oldest surviving chronicle from Japan, recounting the origins of the archipelago and its imperial dynasty.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence opens with a long participial phrase, “Compiled in 712 CE ... had memorized and recited,” that describes the subject, “the Kojiki.” A comma correctly separates this introductory phrase from the main clause “the Kojiki is the oldest surviving chronicle from Japan.”

A.why_wrong: Without a comma, the long introductory phrase runs straight into the main clause, so it is unclear where the phrase ends.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “Compiled in 712 CE ... memorized and recited” is a phrase, not a main clause.

D.why_wrong: The period leaves “Compiled in 712 CE ... had memorized and recited.” as a fragment with no main clause.

items.notes: Subject: literature (early Japanese texts). Medium shape (2.20): a long participial opener whose own relative clause has finite verbs (“had memorized and recited”), so the left side can look complete. Real subject known well.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject and its verb
items.passage: Most frogs and toads deposit their eggs in water and abandon them to develop independently. The eggs that a female Surinam toad carries embedded in the spongy skin of her ______ bypass the free-swimming larval stage entirely, emerging several months later as miniature, fully developed toadlets.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the long noun phrase “The eggs that a female Surinam toad carries embedded in the spongy skin of her back,” and its verb is “bypass.” No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb.

A.why_wrong: The comma separates the subject, “The eggs ... of her back,” from its verb, “bypass.”

B.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause, but “The eggs ... of her back” is only a subject.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “The eggs ... of her back” has no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (amphibians). Medium shape (2.11): a 16-word subject with its own relative clause before the blank, so a pause feels natural. Real subject known well.

fixes: explanation quoted “embedded in the skin of her back”; the passage says “the spongy skin of her back”

items.subtype: Semicolons between list items that contain commas
items.passage: The interior of Qusayr Amra, an eighth-century bathhouse in the Jordanian desert, is decorated with elaborate frescoes, including a hunting scene in which horsemen pursue wild donkeys; a group portrait of six monarchs, among them the rulers of Byzantium and ______ and a domed ceiling depicting the constellations of the zodiac.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three frescoes, and an item contains a comma of its own (“a group portrait of six monarchs, among them ...”), so semicolons separate the items, as the semicolon after “donkeys” shows. A semicolon after “Persia” correctly separates the second item from the third.

A.why_wrong: A comma here doesn’t match the semicolon that separates the first and second items; the items must be separated by semicolons throughout.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the second and third items run together.

D.why_wrong: A colon can’t separate two items in a list.

items.notes: Subject: history (early Islamic art). Medium shape (e2f77ae7): the cue is the semicolon after item 1, 13 words before the blank. Real subject known well.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: The telegraph plant, a shrub native to tropical Asia, is among the few plants whose movements are visible to the naked eye. Its small lateral leaflets rise and fall every few minutes, motions that reminded observers ______ the signaling arms of a semaphore telegraph.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Of” is a preposition, and “the signaling arms of a semaphore telegraph” is its object. No punctuation should separate a preposition from its object.

B.why_wrong: The comma separates the preposition “of” from its object.

C.why_wrong: The dash has no role here; it interrupts the phrase “of the signaling arms.”

D.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause, but “motions that reminded observers of” is not one.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (botany). Easy shape (1.9, 1.22): preposition plus object with comma, dash and colon decoys. Real subject known well.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: For centuries, Indigenous peoples of northeastern North America have made wampum, small purple and white beads cut ______ the shells of whelks and quahog clams. Haudenosaunee nations wove the beads into belts whose patterns recorded agreements, including treaties with European colonists.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “From” is a preposition, and “the shells of whelks and quahog clams” is its object. No punctuation should come between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: The dash has no role here; it interrupts the phrase “from the shells.”

C.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause, but it would come between the preposition “from” and its object.

D.why_wrong: The comma separates the preposition “from” from its object.

items.subtype: Indirect question: statement word order and a period
items.passage: In a traditional folktale about Nasreddin, a comic character familiar from Turkey to Central Asia, a neighbor lends Nasreddin a cooking pot. When it is returned with a smaller pot inside, the neighbor asks why ______ Nasreddin solemnly explains that the pot has given birth.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Why there are now two pots” is an indirect question: it is part of the statement “the neighbor asks why ....” An indirect question uses statement word order (“there are”) and ends with a period, not a question mark.

A.why_wrong: This option uses the inverted word order and question mark of a direct question, but the question is reported inside a statement.

B.why_wrong: The period is right, but an indirect question uses statement word order (“there are”), not inverted order.

D.why_wrong: The word order is right, but the sentence is a statement, so it should end with a period.

items.notes: Subject: literature (folktales). Easy shape (1.7): reported question after “asks why,” full 2 x 2 grid of word order and end mark. Traditional tale, no attribution needed.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: comma plus but
items.passage: The fish-eating bat Myotis vivesi roosts on rocky islands scattered across Mexico’s Gulf of California. Like most bats, it navigates using ______ instead of pursuing insects, it snatches fish from the sea with its elongated, hooked claws.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence joins two main clauses: “Like most bats, it navigates using echolocation” and “instead of pursuing insects, it snatches fish ....” A comma followed by the conjunction “but” correctly joins them and marks the contrast.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two main clauses; without a conjunction, the result is a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together.

C.why_wrong: When “but” joins two main clauses such as these, a comma is needed before it.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (zoology). Easy shape (1.27): splice, fused and conjunction-without-comma menu. Real subject known well.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: The colugo of Southeast Asia glides as far as 100 meters between rainforest trees on a furry membrane stretching from its neck to its tail. Although it is often called a flying ______ animal cannot truly fly and is not a lemur at all.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence opens with the dependent clause “Although it is often called a flying lemur,” which can’t stand on its own. A comma correctly separates it from the main clause “the animal cannot truly fly and is not a lemur at all.”

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but the “Although” clause is dependent.

C.why_wrong: Without a comma, the introductory “Although” clause runs straight into the main clause.

D.why_wrong: The period leaves “Although it is often called a flying lemur.” as a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (zoology). Easy shape (1.8): Although-clause, then the main clause; the options carry the next word as in 1.8. Real subject known well (colugos glide on a skin membrane and form their own order, not lemurs).

items.subtype: Commas between items of a simple series

items.explanation: The sentence lists three items: “magnesium,” “calcium,” and “sodium sulfates.” Items in a simple list are separated by commas, so a comma belongs after “magnesium.”

A.why_wrong: Without a comma, the first two items of the list run together.

C.why_wrong: Semicolons separate list items only when the items contain commas of their own; these items don’t.

D.why_wrong: A colon can’t separate two items in a list.
